name: Opus-fleet dividend growth
strategy: Concentrated in 25+ year dividend aristocrats and quality dividend-grower ETFs with defensive staples/healthcare tilt, funded by strong free cash flow, harvesting 4% cash yield on the sleeve.

positions.thesis: Held flat at 40% for the third straight week, and this time the flat hold has an active macro reason rather than only a refusal. A Fed that is hiking because inflation will not come down is a Fed that raises the discount rate on long-duration cash flows and rewards cash flow received now — which is mechanically what the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 index screens for. That rotation is already the dominant fact of this fund's year: +27.9% YTD against the S&P's +13.85%, which is market leadership moving from mega-cap technology into value and dividend payers, not a lucky quarter. Warsh's speech makes that leadership more likely to persist, so the largest thing I own is also the thing most aligned with the regime I now expect. I still will not add to it, and the reason is the same one I gave last week and re-verified this week: its top three holdings are ABT at 4.86%, MRK at 4.82% and AMGN at 4.75%, roughly 14.4% of the fund in three names the sell-side puts at or through fair value, with 21.04% of the fund in healthcare overall. Buying more SCHD would deepen the valuation compression and the sector concentration I spent this week reducing elsewhere. What it keeps: $104.31B AUM, 0.06% fee, a 2.89% forward yield, a 0.69 beta, 101 holdings, and a mechanical quarterly rotation toward cash-flow quality that requires no opinion from me. That is a rebalancing basket, not a momentum position, so its all-time high is information rather than a signal. The 12% stop stays what it is — catastrophe protection on a 100-name vehicle, not a trading stop — and there is still no take-profit, because you do not take profits on the compounding core.

Held flat at 9% for the second week, and the reason is again the calendar, now at one day's distance: Q1 FY2027 reports Tuesday September 1 before the open. On the scorecard it improved this week — the stock fell 2.3% to $91.22 while the $98.44 consensus from 29 analysts held, so upside widened from 5.45% to 7.92% and the score rose to 11.1, tied for third-best in the book at a 3.16% yield. Last week I said it wanted more weight and the calendar was the only thing stopping me. That is still true, and options-implied pricing puts the earnings move at roughly 4%, which means adding today to capture a 2% better entry is paying a coin-flip for a rounding error. The bar Tuesday is real but not stretched: $1.38-$1.39 EPS against $1.26 a year ago, revenue up 4-6%, with the FY27 guide $5.90-$6.00 and roughly $75M of tariff cost landing in the quarter against ~$250M for the year, about 20bp of gross margin. What I need to see is the Affera pulsed-field ablation ramp and Hugo adoption converting, because the whole thesis is that 15.7x forward against 25.0x trailing means the street has modelled an earnings recovery that reported numbers have not yet shown — the margin-lag signature of a turnaround mid-flight, with revenue growing 8.43% while net income grew 2.98%. At a 0.57 beta this is the book's designated low-beta ballast, the role I moved it into when I retired JNJ. I am keeping the 10% stop rather than widening it into the print, even knowing a stop can be gapped through: at a 4% implied move the stop sits about 2.5 standard deviations out, and I said last week the tight stop was there precisely because of September 1. Loosening a stop the week it might actually be needed would be the rule that binds only when it is free. Take-profit at +10% is near $100.3, above the $98.44 consensus, where a genuine beat-and-raise lands and a drift does not.

Raised from 7% back to 9%, reversing the trim I made two weeks ago, and I want to be exact about why this is not the thing I refused to do last week. The rule I bound myself to was narrow and I will quote its logic: having flagged the Middle East geopolitical premium as this position's one-headline reversal risk, and having banked two points when that risk became an actual headline, I would not re-underwrite one week later at a HIGHER price merely because the market shrugged. That rule was about not chasing. It is not in force here on either half. The price is $201.86, which is $3.41 BELOW the $205.27 where I declined to buy last week and below where I trimmed. And the reason is genuinely new rather than the absence of bad news: Warsh's hawkish turn, the single biggest market event of the week, was driven by inflation that is substantially energy-led — Brent closed at $88.68 with WTI near $83, the Iran war unresolved, Hormuz disruption ongoing, and Russia-Ukraine escalation opening a second supply front, with the Dallas Fed publishing on exactly this channel. That makes energy the one sleeve in an income book that a hiking Fed helps rather than compresses, because the commodity causing the tightening is the same commodity that pays this company. On my own scorecard it also earns the capital independently: 3.53% yield plus 7.6% upside to a $217.23 consensus from 31 analysts, score 11.1, at 13.3x forward with a 0.49 beta, with Morgan Stanley lifting to $218 on August 19. The franchise keeps delivering — the 105-4X condensate discovery in Angola's Block 0, Equinor taking 17.4% of the offshore Namibia license. I stop at 9% and not higher because the one-headline risk cuts both ways: a ceasefire crushes the premium as fast as an escalation built it, which is exactly why the 10% stop stays. Take-profit holds at +8%, about $218, right at consensus and just through the $214.71 52-week high — reachable on a crude spike, not on drift.

Cut from 10% to 5%, the second consecutive trim, and it is the same rule that took KO from 13 to 9 to 5 applied to myself without an exemption for a name I like. I went into this week expecting to ADD. The stock fell 3.0% from my $264.96 mark to $256.99 on no fundamental break, which on last week's logic — I sized it at 13% for the widest gap in the book and cut to 10% when the gap closed to 4.39% — should have reopened the gap and earned the weight back. It did not. The consensus fell with the price: the same 31-analyst S&P Global panel that read $276.59 a week ago now reads $266.89, so upside is 3.85%, slightly WORSE than when I trimmed. Two other panels are worse still, with 40 analysts averaging $256.53 and 29 averaging $252.90, meaning the broadest coverage puts this stock at or through fair value. Targets falling faster than the price is deterioration in the sell-side's view, not a discount. On my two axes it now scores 6.5 — 2.69% yield on a $6.92 payout plus 3.85% upside — the lowest number in this book, while holding my single largest name weight. I wrote last week that paying up for a name trading 4% from consensus is precisely what I am selling elsewhere; holding 10% of one is the same error wearing a nicer suit. The business is not why I am selling and I will not pretend otherwise: Q2 beat on both lines, revenue guidance was raised again, Skyrizi, Rinvoq and neuroscience are all growing, forward PE is 17.5 with the 74.9 trailing being IPR&D accounting noise, and the 53-year raise streak is genuine aristocracy. The stock is -4.4% since the 7/31 print purely because Apogee dilution took the FY26 EPS guide to $13.87-$14.07 from $13.91-$14.11 — a known, quantified, four-cent issue the market is charging far more than four cents for. The second reason for the cut is one I only found by re-pulling holdings: SCHD is 21.04% healthcare with ABT, MRK and AMGN as its top three, so ABBV at 10% plus MDT at 9% put ~27% of NAV in one sector I never explicitly chose to bet on. This takes it to ~22%. No income is forfeited — the next ex-dividend is not until roughly October 12-15. Take-profit resets to +5%, near $270, just through the $266.89 consensus and therefore a fillable order rather than a wish; the 10% stop stands.

Held flat at 5% in its first full week, down 2.3% to $140.13, and holding flat is a decision I nearly got wrong. It is now the highest-scoring security in the book at 14.8 — a 4.16% yield plus 10.6% upside to a $155 consensus, with MarketBeat's panel at $157.90 — and a mechanical reading of my own scorecard says double it. Two things stopped me. First, I ran down a catalyst and it failed the date check: a Citi raise to $170 from $165 looked like the downgrade cycle turning, which was the exact condition I sized small for, but that raise is from December 2025 and Citigroup then CUT to $145 on July 10, 2026. The Hold-with-active-downgrades condition I underwrote is unchanged, so adding on it would have been adding on a stale headline. Second, and this is the week's discipline, PEP is a bond proxy and the Fed just signalled a September hike at ~60% odds; buying duration into that on a scorecard reading is exactly the mechanical behaviour I try to catch in myself. What is real and current is the restructuring: PepsiCo has now FORMALIZED its agreement with Elliott's ~$4B stake to cut the US product lineup by 20% with price resets on core brands, alongside Frito-Lay closures in Orlando, Rancho Cucamonga and Liberty NY, against a 2-4% organic revenue growth guide. That is a named margin catalyst not yet in the tape, and it is why 16.5x forward for a 54-year raiser sitting 18% below its $171.48 high with a freshly declared 4% increase is a thesis being priced rather than a thesis breaking — the distinction I drew when I bought this and sold P&G. Frito-Lay volume weakness and North American snacking behaviour remain the genuine bear case and I am not burying it. I collect the September 4 ex-dividend. Next earnings are October 8, well past the next reassessment, so the 12% stop stays deliberately wide: I do not want to be shaken out of a 4%-plus yield by tape noise while a restructuring works. Take-profit moves UP from +12% to +14%, near $159.7, purely to preserve the original design — because the price fell, the same dollar target now needs a larger percentage to stay above the $155-$157.90 consensus band, where a real North America inflection re-rates the multiple rather than merely closing the target gap.

Held flat at 5%, and this is the position the week's news is aimed squarely at. When I bought it seven days ago I named rate duration as its specific accepted risk and said I was taking it knowingly because the alternative use of the capital was cash at 4% while O pays 120bp more with three decades of raises attached. Warsh has now moved a September hike to roughly 60% probability, so that named risk went from ambient to likely inside one week. My own precedent with CVX says the disciplined response to a flagged risk materialising is to reduce rather than re-underwrite. I am not reducing, and the distinction is that with CVX the risk had materialised in the PRICE and I had a gain to bank; here it has materialised only in probability, the stock is down about 1% to $61.98, and one Jackson Hole speech moving futures from 56% to 60% is not the event, the September 16-17 FOMC is. Selling a 5.24% contractual yield on a four-point shift in an options-implied probability is over-trading a duration risk I explicitly chose to carry, and it would also forfeit Monday's August 31 ex-dividend of $0.271, payable September 15. On the merits nothing has broken and something improved: Q2 2026 revenue of $1.55B beat on robust investment activity, management RAISED full-year guidance to $4.44-$4.45 EPS against a $4.43 consensus, and the consensus target is $67.42 for 8.8% upside, so I am still buying into an upgrade cycle rather than a value trap. The 'funded by strong free cash flow' clause of my mandate is met more literally here than anywhere else in the book: contractual net-lease rent from 15,500-plus properties across 50 states and nine countries, tenanted toward grocery, convenience, dollar and drug stores, which is staples exposure by revenue source even though the wrapper is a REIT. Thirty consecutive annual increases and 674 consecutive monthly dividends is the longest unbroken payment record I own. The honest caveats stand: the 45.8x headline P/E is a REIT depreciation artifact with AFFO in the low-to-mid teens being the real multiple, and the consensus rating is Hold. Rate risk is now live and monitored rather than theoretical, which is precisely why this stays at 5% and does not grow despite scoring 14.0. The 10% stop is the mechanism that makes carrying the duration survivable if the long end backs up hard; take-profit at +10%, about $68.2, sits just through consensus.

Held flat at 5% after two consecutive cuts, and flat is now correct for the same reason the cuts were. I took it 13 to 9 to 5 on the stated principle that I should hold the weight I would actually initiate; at $89.66, down 1.6% on the week, it scores 8.0 — a 2.36% yield plus 5.62% upside to a $94.70 consensus from 24 analysts, with a $96 median and a $75-$104 range — which is second-worst in the book but genuinely better than the 3.95% upside that triggered the last cut, because the stock came off the $91.87 52-week high it had been pressed against. That is enough to own at 5% and not enough to own at more, so the position is exactly where my rule puts it and I am leaving it there rather than trading a name twice in three weeks for a point of scorecard. The business justifies the floor: FY26 guidance was raised on the Q2 print, 2025 earnings rose 23.29% on 1.87% revenue growth, EPS is up 18.0% to $3.33, volume and organic growth are intact, several firms pushed targets above $95 after the quarter, and the 62-year streak is the longest raise record among my direct equity lines — a Dividend King and the reason this holds a permanent seat in an aristocrat mandate. The fairlife cybersecurity incident resolved with production resumed and stays a contained subsidiary event. The pressure point is valuation into a hiking Fed: near 27x forward for a 2.36% yield, this is the most expensive bond proxy I own per unit of income, and a rising discount rate is precisely what a 27x multiple on 2% revenue growth cannot absorb. That is why the 8% stop stays the tightest in the book and why the take-profit moves only from +5% to +6%, to about $95.0 — the previous level had drifted just BELOW the $94.70 consensus as the stock fell, and a take-profit that fills before the analyst number is reached is leaving money on the table for no reason. At +6% it sits just through consensus, in the zone where the post-Q2 target raises actually landed.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Two things changed and they point the same way. First, ABBV failed a test I apply symmetrically: I cut KO twice on the stated rule that a name I would not initiate at its current upside cannot hold an above-initiation weight by default, and ABBV is now the lowest-scoring name I own (2.69% yield + 3.85% upside = 6.5 against a book median near 11) while carrying my largest single-name weight at 10%. I expected its gap to have reopened after a 3% price fall; instead the same 31-analyst panel cut its target from $276.59 to $266.89, so the gap narrowed. The property I paid the weight for is gone in both directions now, so the weight goes to 5% — the tier where KO, PEP and O sit, meaning worth owning and not worth overweighting. It also fixes a concentration I had not deliberately chosen: SCHD is 21.04% healthcare with ABT, MRK and AMGN as its top three, so at 40% SCHD plus ABBV 10% plus MDT 9% I was running ~27% of NAV in one sector. Second, the Fed turned. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech put a September 25bp HIKE at ~60% odds, and the inflation he is chasing is energy-led with Brent at $88.68, the Iran war unresolved and Hormuz still disrupted. That raises my cash hurdle, compresses every bond-proxy multiple I own, and helps exactly one sleeve. So 2 points of the 5 go back into CVX, my only energy line, and 3 points go to cash at a risk-free rate that is about to rise. I am deliberately NOT pushing the freed capital into PEP and O, which score highest on my scorecard at 14.8 and 14.0, because they are the two longest-duration things I own and buying duration one day after the Fed signals a hike is scorecard-following with the macro switched off. Gross falls 81% to 78%; net equity risk is barely changed, its composition is better.
novelty: I manage only a Round-3 book in this experiment, so no Round-2 overlap constraint binds; the construction remains distinct on its own terms — a 40% rules-based dividend core plus six aristocrat-tier single names, no leverage, no shorts, no crypto, and a deliberately large cash sleeve sized off the risk-free rate rather than off residual capital.
research_notes:
PRICES AT 2026-08-28 CLOSE (verified individually): SCHD $34.90 (+0.20% Fri), ABBV $256.99, MDT $91.22, CVX $201.86, PEP $140.13, O $61.98, KO $89.66. My whole equity book pulled back roughly 1-3% on the week; NAV $1,050.38, +5.04% since inception, max DD -2.39%. No stop or take-profit fired.

THE WEEK'S ONE MATERIAL EVENT — THE FED. Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech on 2026-08-28 was unexpectedly hawkish: he said recent inflation data gave "little comfort," that underlying trends have not improved, and that "markets are showing few signs of policy restraint." Fed funds futures now price a 57-60% chance of a 25bp HIKE at the mid-September meeting, up from ~56% pre-speech. S&P closed Friday -0.25% (7,712) on it, giving back part of a +0.49% week that had been driven by NVDA's +8.7% post-earnings move. This is a regime input for an income book, not noise: it raises my cash yield (4% APY and rising), raises the discount rate on every bond-proxy multiple I own, and specifically re-prices the duration in O and the staples.

WHY THE FED IS HAWKISH MATTERS FOR MY BOOK. The inflation Warsh is reacting to is substantially energy-led: Brent closed near $88.68 and WTI near $83 on 8/28 with the Iran war ongoing, Strait of Hormuz disruption unresolved, and Russia-Ukraine escalation now adding a second supply front. The Dallas Fed has a working paper out specifically on the 2026 Iran war's impact on US inflation. So the single sleeve a hawkish, energy-driven Fed helps rather than hurts is the one I own the least of.

UPDATED SCORECARD (yield + upside to consensus, the two axes my mandate runs on), which re-widened materially this week from last week's compressed 2.37%-6.14% upside band:
- PEP: $140.13, 4.16% yield, $155 consensus (S&P Global, 24 analysts) to $157.90 (MarketBeat) = 10.6% upside. Score 14.8.
- O: $61.98, 5.24% yield ($3.252 annualized), $67.42 consensus = 8.8% upside. Score 14.0.
- CVX: $201.86, 3.53% yield, $217.23 consensus (31 analysts), Morgan Stanley raised to $218 on 8/19 = 7.6% upside. Score 11.1.
- MDT: $91.22, 3.16% yield, $98.44 consensus = 7.9% upside. Score 11.1.
- KO: $89.66, 2.36% yield, $94.70 consensus (24 analysts) = 5.6% upside. Score 8.0.
- ABBV: $256.99, 2.69% yield ($6.92), $266.89 consensus (S&P Global, 31 analysts) = 3.85% upside. Score 6.5. Two other panels are worse: 40 analysts average $256.53 (zero upside), 29 analysts average $252.90 (negative).

THE ABBV FINDING IS THE WEEK'S REAL WORK. I expected the opposite. ABBV fell 3.0% from my $264.96 mark with no fundamental break, so the naive read was that the valuation gap I trimmed on had reopened and I should add back. It has not. The consensus came DOWN with the price — the same 31-analyst panel that read $276.59 last week now reads $266.89 — so the gap actually narrowed slightly, from 4.39% to 3.85%. Targets fell faster than the stock. The cause is unchanged and known: the Apogee Therapeutics dilution cut FY26 EPS guidance to $13.87-$14.07 from $13.91-$14.11, and the stock is -4.4% since the 7/31 Q2 print despite that print beating on revenue and earnings with Skyrizi, Rinvoq and neuroscience all strong and revenue guidance raised again. Checking this is what stopped me making the wrong trade.

CONCENTRATION I HAD NOT PRICED. I re-pulled SCHD's holdings: ABT 4.86%, MRK 4.82%, AMGN 4.75%, top ten 41.61% of the fund, $104.3B AUM, and 21.04% healthcare — the fund's single largest sector. On a 40% SCHD weight that is 8.4% of NAV in healthcare before I own a single drug stock directly. Add ABBV 10% and MDT 9% and I was carrying ~27% of NAV in healthcare on an 81% gross book. That is a sector bet I never explicitly decided to make.

MDT EARNINGS ARE TUESDAY. Q1 FY2027 reports 2026-09-01 before the open — one trading day after this reassessment. Consensus $1.38-$1.39 EPS (up ~9.5-10.3% y/y) on $8.2-9.5B revenue; FY27 guide $5.90-$6.00. Bloomberg-compiled options data implies roughly a 4% move. Watch items: Affera pulsed-field ablation ramp, Hugo robotic adoption, SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular integration, and ~$75M of Q1 tariff cost (~$250M FY, ~20bp of gross margin).

PEP CATALYST CHECKED AND PARTLY DEBUNKED. A search surfaced "Citi raises PEP target to $170 from $165," which would have been a real change to the downgrade cycle I sized around. It is stale — that raise was December 2025, and Citigroup CUT PEP from $170 to $145 on 2026-07-10. So the Hold-with-downgrades condition I sized at 5% for still holds and I am not doubling the position on a phantom upgrade. What IS real and current: PepsiCo has formalized its restructuring agreement with Elliott (~$4B stake) to cut the US product lineup by 20% with price resets on core brands, plus Frito-Lay plant closures in Orlando, Rancho Cucamonga and Liberty NY, against a 2-4% organic revenue growth guide. Real catalyst, not yet in the tape. Ex-dividend 9/4, which I collect.

INCOME CALENDAR: O goes ex-dividend Monday 8/31 ($0.271 monthly, paid 9/15) — a reason not to touch that leg this week. PEP ex-div 9/4. SCHD's latest distribution was $0.25 (8/30), forward yield 2.89%. ABBV's next ex-div is not until ~10/12-10/15, so trimming it now forfeits no income. SCHD is +27.9% YTD versus the S&P's +13.85%, which is a genuine value/dividend leadership rotation rather than a fluke, and a hiking Fed that punishes long-duration growth is more likely to extend that rotation than end it.
